It is extensive in its coverage as it attempts to exhaust a large proportion of protections that are provided to indigenous knowledge specialities such as heritage protection, Africa's Scientific Technical Indigenous Knowledge (STIK) protections, indigenous designs, indigenous literary knowledge, sign terms and expressions and various cultural expressions in the African audiovisual industry and indigenous African music.

title: WTO Safeguards in Africa: Limited Use, Compliance Challenges and Capacity Constraints
author: Gustav Brink
summary: Safeguards are one of three World Trade Organization (WTO)-sanctioned trade remedies that countries may use to protect their domestic industries against various forms of increased international competition. However, few African countries make use of the instrument, with only Egypt, Madagascar, Morocco and South Africa as active users, while three more countries have each conducted a single safeguard investigation. There are some WTO inconsistencies in the way each of these countries conduct safeguard investigations, but nothing that cannot be addressed without too much effort. Other African countries, especially the more industrialised countries such as Kenya, Nigeria and Tanzania, should finalise their safeguards legislation and request technical assistance from the WTO and the African countries actively using the instrument to rapidly upskill to allow themselves to use the instrument. Safeguards can be instrumental in protecting domestic industries against increased imports and allow them the opportunity to adjust to such increased competition, thereby enabling African countries to participate more fully in international trade and beneficiate raw materials domestically, all of which could contribute to Africa’s economic growth.

title: Educational Standards, Qualifications and Competency Frameworks for Councillors in South African Municipalities—A Constitutional Need
author: Nonhlanhla Ngcobo
summary: The Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (CoGTA) is currently reviewing the 1998 White Paper on Local Government, marking the beginning of a new era for a sphere whose constitutional and legislative powers have significantly contributed to the development of local communities. Despite this recognition, local government continues to face persistent challenges, including deficiencies in administrative governance, service delivery backlogs, infrastructure constraints, and both financial and structural limitations. However, the review of the White Paper fails to acknowledge that many of these challenges can be significantly attributed to the low literacy levels of councillors—the key decision-makers in municipalities—among other factors. This omission persists despite the minister’s public admission that more than 300 councillors in the KwaZulu-Natal Province are unable to read or write. This article argues that the absence of minimum educational, expertise and competency requirements for councillors may undermine the effective implementation of the proposed reforms, especially given the increasing complexity of political, financial and administrative tasks and decision-making within the local government sphere. The article undertakes a critical analysis of political rights and principles enshrined in the Constitution in the context of the dysfunctional local government in South Africa, and in response, offers a carefully crafted councillor competency capacity development framework that does not encroach on the relevant constitutional guarantees.

title: Eligibility of Victims of International Crimes for Reparations before the International Criminal Court: A Critique
author: Bongani M Dlamini, Linda Mushoriwa
summary: The adoption of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court on 17 July 1998 and the establishment of the International Criminal Court (ICC or the Court) on 2 July 2002 marked a significant turn for international criminal justice. Notably, the Court established a platform for bringing justice to victims of international crimes, whilst putting the victims at the centre of proceedings. One way in which this is evident is the framework for awarding reparations to victims of the core crimes of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. This not only serves to acknowledge the victims’ pain and suffering but also to remedy the harm they have suffered. The Court’s mandate to award reparations to victims of international crimes is provided for in Article 75 of the Rome Statute. The purpose of this article is to examine the Court’s reparations regime with respect to the eligibility of victims to receive reparations as provided for in the Rome Statute, and as seen through the lens of the Court’s jurisprudence on this subject. The article asserts that whilst the reparations regime is an innovative way to deliver justice to victims of atrocities, its effectiveness remains subject to debate due to challenges associated with the interpretation of the meaning of ‘victims’ for purposes of reparations, and the eligibility criteria for victims to be awarded reparations. It concludes that the Court must consider amending its procedural laws to allow flexibility and place more prominence on the content of reparations delivered in individual cases.
publication: Comparative and International Law Journal of Southern Africa

title: Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation in Zimbabwe: Lessons from South Africa
author: Basutu S Makwaiba
summary: The purpose of this article is to critically review the judicial approach to delegated legislation in Zimbabwe. One of the firmly entrenched principles in constitutional law is that legislative power cannot be delegated. The limitation on the legislature’s delegation of its primary law-making powers is based on the doctrine of non-delegation. The non-delegation doctrine commands that the legislature alone exercise law-making power. This article examines the extent to which the Zimbabwean courts have enforced the non-delegation doctrine when reviewing executive law-making under the Presidential Powers (Temporary Measures) Act. The courts have held that the Act is constitutional even though it assigns Parliament’s primary law-making to the executive. The article used a doctrinal research methodology to analyse existing primary and secondary sources. It also included a desk review, which employed a comparative methodology. The comparative analysis focused on South Africa, selected for its judiciary’s ability to exert stronger oversight over the delegation of legislative authority to the executive. The South African courts have defined the limits to which legislative powers may be delegated distinguishing between delegation to make subordinate legislation and assigning primary law-making power to another body. This article aims to contribute to the existing literature on the nature and extent of constitutional limitations on the delegation of legislative powers. There is a conspicuous dearth of scholarly literature examining judicial oversight of delegated legislation in Zimbabwe, and this study addresses that gap.
publication: Comparative and International Law Journal of Southern Africa

title: Public versus stakeholder engagement: A distinction for policy-makers to avoid undue interference
author: Sameera Mahomedy, Darshen Naidoo
publication: South African Journal on Human Rights

title: Accountable Predictive Policing of Cybercrime? Insights from Nigerian Law Enforcement
author: Ifeoma Nwafor
summary: The unconventional challenges in cybercrime investigation and mitigation brought about by the sophistication of Artificial Intelligence (AI) significantly impact the fight against cybercrime. Cybercriminals employ AI and machine learning to bypass cybersecurity defences and expand cyber threats. There is an active and ongoing debate on how AI can enable defenders to detect, predict and effectively respond to cyber threats using AI technologies such as predictive policing tools. However, the effectiveness of predictive policing has not been widely accepted in scientific and contemporary literature due to human rights, legal and ethical concerns that inhibit its employment in cybercrime mitigation. There is a remarkable magnitude of cybercrime in Nigeria, perpetrated by Nigerians globally, compared to other countries. Nigeria ranks 5th globally as a source of cybercrime and cybercriminal activity, according to the world's first Cybercrime Index. Nigeria also ranked 13th as the most vulnerable country to cyberattacks on the Global Threat Index. Nigerian law enforcement agencies are ill-equipped to confront the technological advancements in cybercrime. This study, based on qualitative and desk research, explores the necessary adaptation of existing predictive policing techniques to the Nigerian cybercrime situation, taking into account the problematisation of what predictive policing represents today. It conducts a criminological analysis of the law enforcement response to cybercrime in Nigeria, highlighting the role of digitalisation in cybercrime prevention in the country. Additionally, it examines the legal status of predictive policing technologies in Nigeria, including their compliance and risk management considerations. Based on insights from Nigerian law enforcement, this study found that predictive policing is not a preventive measure for combating cybercrime in Nigeria due to legal, ethical, and human rights concerns inherent in such AI-driven tools across all domains of their usage. Findings reveal that the legal status of predictive policing systems in Nigeria remains ambiguous, as there is no dedicated AI governance and regulatory framework governing their legal position and use. Additionally, formal measurement or oversight of compliance and risk management regarding predictive policing deployment in Nigerian law enforcement is limited and largely ad hoc due to the absence of specific AI regulation in Nigeria.

title: Centering Intellectual Property in Artificial Intelligence Strategies in Africa Through a Techno-legal Analysis
author: Desmond Oriakhogba
summary: Policy-makers at the regional and national levels in Africa are formulating strategies to develop and take charge of the regional and national artificial intelligence (AI) ecosystems towards achieving the sustainable development objectives set out in their respective development plans. The African Union has a continental AI strategy, while eleven African countries have developed national AI strategies. Given its significance to AI development in Africa, it is important to reflect on how best intellectual property (IP) should be approached in AI strategies in Africa: should policy-makers develop new IP rules for AI, or revise or simply implement existing IP rules within the AI context? Resolving these questions requires a firm understanding of the key AI- and IP-related issues in the African context examined through a techno-legal lens. Adopting a qualitative methodology by way of policy review, this paper unpacks the issues by reviewing existing African regional and national AI strategies. It refers to relevant judicial and policy developments in the United States of America, China, Australia and Europe to draw comparative insights on the research question. The paper contends that the resolution of the question of whether new IP rules should be developed for AI, and whether existing IP rules should be revised or simply implemented within the AI context depends on the AI-IP issue in focus. Whatever the case, an approach to IP in AI strategies which is human-centered, development-focused, and equitably balances the promotion of AI innovation by enabling access to quality data with the protection of IP rights while also securing just reward for creators, innovators and indigenous communities will position Africa to more effectively leverage AI towards national and regional development.

title: Towards an African Union Treaty on Artificial Intelligence: Reconciling African Values with Global Standards
author: Lukman Abdulrauf
summary: In the wake of the European Union (EU)'s landmark Artificial Intelligence Act and similar normative developments in other regions, the regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) has become a global race for governance legitimacy and leadership. While many jurisdictions are swiftly advancing binding legislative instruments to manage the opportunities and risks of AI, AI governance across African states and regional institutions has, to date, tended to favour a more deliberative and consultative approach, reflecting diverse national priorities and capacities. The African Union (AU), through various soft law initiatives and continental strategies, has established foundational principles that prioritise inclusiveness, context sensitivity, and sovereignty in technological governance. Chief among these initiatives is the AU Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy, which articulates a vision for AI governance that reflects African values – a collection of indigenous values, a communal ethos, and socio-cultural realities – while cautiously engaging with the technical universality promoted by global standards. The purpose of this paper is to outline an agenda for discussions on the imperative and feasibility of transitioning from soft law frameworks to an AU treaty on AI. It argues that the central challenge is not merely the codification of rules, but the normative reconciliation of African values with existing global standards. Global AI standards – often shaped by Eurocentric epistemologies and market logic – may inadequately reflect African ethical frameworks, historical contexts and development priorities. Yet the pursuit of regulatory autonomy must not lead to technological isolationism. Instead, the article argues for a hybrid normative approach that retains the technical interoperability necessary for international collaboration, while embedding the African philosophies of Ubuntu, solidarity and fairness within the legal architecture of AI governance.

title: Towards a Transdisciplinary Governance of Artificial Intelligence in Africa
author: CI Okorie
summary: The governance of artificial intelligence (AI) in Africa faces competing pressures from demands for regulatory intervention alongside concerns about institutional capacity, innovation costs, and economic vulnerability. Debates surrounding algorithmic discrimination, biometric surveillance, and extractive data practices by global platforms have sharpened questions about the appropriate roles of states, markets, and civil society in governing AI systems. Yet existing governance scholarship tends to address these questions through either ethical principles or state-centric regulatory frameworks, leaving a significant analytical gap where law and technical design intersect. This article introduces legal-technical governance as an analytical framework for examining Africa’s emerging AI regulatory landscape. Distinguishing governance from regulation, the article argues that AI governance in Africa is already distributed across data protection statutes, fintech guidelines, cybersecurity frameworks, and content moderation policies imposed by global platforms, making a broader, systems-level analytical tool both necessary and timely. Legal-technical governance foregrounds the co-constitutive relationship between legal norms and technical operations, including data labelling, model training, and algorithmic auditing. It accounts for the various actors shaping AI outcomes, from multinational technology firms to standards bodies and affected communities. To examine the gaps where legal frameworks and technical systems diverge, the article draws on Dooyeweerd's modal aspects as a philosophical lens. Applied to African AI governance domains, this framework reveals how institutional fragmentation, infrastructural dependency, and global platform dominance undermine state-centred regulatory models. The article concludes by advancing legal-technical governance as a productive framework for scholarship and policymaking at the intersection of law, technology, and development in Africa.

title: Bridging the Legal-technical Gap: AI Surveillance and Data Sovereignty in Africa
author: Maria Lungu
summary: South African and Nigerian law guarantees rights to privacy and due process, but national security carve-outs and proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) systems shielded from regulatory scrutiny can make those protections difficult to enforce. As African governments progressively rely on foreign vendors for AI-enabled surveillance technologies, a central question is how constitutional protections can be meaningfully enforced when the systems governing surveillance remain technically and legally inaccessible to domestic oversight. The theoretical contribution is the concept of the algorithmic sovereignty gap, which names the persistent disjunction between constitutional guarantees and the operational realities of vendor-controlled tools. Drawing on qualitative content analysis of constitutional law, statutes, case law, and investigative reporting in both countries, and extending Pasquale's black-box problem and Couldry and Mejias's data colonialism framework through a postcolonial lens, the article shows how procurement-led deployment and security exceptions hollow out constitutional rights that the legal texts appear to guarantee. The prescriptive contribution is a hybrid governance model that closes this gap by anchoring transparency and accountability in constitutional baselines, supported by mandatory AI impact assessments, audit rights, source-code escrow, data localisation, and procurement transparency.

title: Editorial: Legal-Technical Governance and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in Africa
author: Chijioke Okorie, Vukosi Marivate
summary: This editorial introduces the special issue on the legal-technical governance and regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) in Africa, the product of a project launched by the Data Science Law Lab in collaboration with the Data Science for Social Impact research group at the University of Pretoria. It situates the five peer-reviewed contributions within a legal-technical approach to AI governance: a transdisciplinary approach in which the legal and the technical are fused to add nuance to regulatory forms and practices and to close the legal-technical gap in AI governance and regulation. The contributions move from conceptual foundations, where legal-technical governance is advanced as an analytical framework, through continental norm-making on the transition from African Union soft law to an AI treaty and national policy design on intellectual property in African AI strategies, to the operation of AI systems in practice, addressing the algorithmic sovereignty gap in AI-enabled surveillance in South Africa and Nigeria and the legal status of predictive policing in the fight against cybercrime in Nigeria.

title: About Understatement Penalties, the Burden of Proof, <i>Bona Fide</i> Inadvertent Errors, and Blameworthiness
author: Stephanus Phillipus Van Zyl, Carolina Meyer, Sascha Kreft
summary: The purpose of understatement penalties in the Tax Administration Act 28 of 2011 (TAA) is twofold – it serves as a deterrent, and it serves a compensatory purpose to make good the loss suffered by the South African Revenue Service because of the understatement. In respect of the compensatory purpose, it resembles delict. As such, the authors draw from the commonalities between understatement penalties and delict to argue that understatement penalties constitute a statutory claim for damages. Accordingly, an analogy between the burden of proof in a claim for damages and the burden of proof in the case of understatement penalties must be drawn. This analogy forms the basis for the arguments that section 223 of the TAA does not create a shift in the burden of proof in that the taxpayer must prove the presence of a bona fide inadvertent error. The contribution also discusses the interpretation of a bona fide inadvertent error and makes some recommendations in this regard.

title: ESTA Occupiers and the Construction of Buildings and Homesteads on Farmland: Addressing Critical Issues in Light of <i>Prinsloo NO v Ngcongwane</i> [2023] ZALCC 22 and Basfour 3327 (Pty) Ltd v Thwala (Leave to Appeal) [2023] ZALCC 28
author: Lerato Rudolph Ngwenyama
summary: The purpose of the Extension of Security of Tenure Act (62 of 1997) (ESTA) is to enhance and promote the ideal of long-term security of tenure for occupiers of land on an equitable basis, promote land-tenure reform as a means of redressing the results of past discrimination and facilitate land-tenure justice. The history of land dispossession and labour tenancy is important to this context and connects with the purpose of ESTA. To fulfil the purpose of ESTA as contemplated in the Preamble, the objects of ESTA are, among others, to afford certain rights and duties to persons who reside on land that they do not own.

author: Lerato Rudolph Ngwenyama
summary: The purpose of the Extension of Security of Tenure Act (62 of 1997) (ESTA) is to enhance and promote the ideal of long-term security of tenure for occupiers of land on an equitable basis, promote land-tenure reform as a means of redressing the results of past discrimination and facilitate land-tenure justice. title: Lawyers are Safe from the AI Invasion—For Now! A Brief Consideration of the Use of Artificially Generated Tools in Legal Research in SA and the US
author: Ciresh Singh, Menelisi Ncube
summary: A legal maxim holds that ‘it is not knowing all the law that counts but knowing where to find the law that makes a good lawyer a great lawyer,’ highlighting the importance of legal research. While technology and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed research and drafting, they are prone to errors, including fabricated authorities. Courts, especially in the United States (US), have sanctioned misuse and South African courts have raised concerns, though no regulations yet exist. This paper examines AI use in legal research by undertaking a detailed analysis of the recent case law, in the US and South Africa, that has considered this topic. This paper will be divided into five parts: Part 1 serves as an introduction and overview of the topic; Part 2 briefly considers some of the AI tools currently available and their possible application in legal practice; Part 3 investigates how some AI tools have been used in the US; Part 4 considers the use of AI tools in the South African legal system; and Part 5 serves as a conclusion and provides some key recommendations in this area. It is hoped that this discussion will bring to light the need for AI regulation and, possibly, the prompt implementation of guidelines and rules to regulate its use not only in legal practice, but also in society. The article draws on both primary and secondary materials and employs a qualitative desktop research method. This article calls for, inter alia, concerted efforts by the legislature and other relevant stakeholders to comprehensively regulate the use of AI by legal practitioners when conducting legal research in order to retain the integrity of the South African legal profession.
publication: Comparative and International Law Journal of Southern Africa

title: Integration of AI tools into management and governance of humanitarian projects in conflict-affected North-West Nigeria
author: Akaninyene O. Unaam, Etini A. Unaam
summary: <jats:p>Humanitarian projects in conflict zones face extreme complexity caused by, inter alia, volatility, fragmentation, and accountability pressures. Such complexity often renders conventional project implementation approaches inadequate. This study, focused on the conflict zone of North-West Nigeria, investigated the extent to which artificial intelligence (AI) tools can enhance the effectiveness of management governance and governance of humanitarian projects. Grounded in sociotechnical systems (STS) theory, the study surveyed 300 project personnel across Kebbi, Katsina, and Jigawa States, and conducted interviews with 25 of the personnel. Statistical analysis of the quantitative data from the survey found that the adoption of AI tools had a statistically significant correlation with project management effectiveness (β = .46, p < .001), with organisational readiness and ethical governance found to serve as significant partial mediators. The qualitative findings from the interview data identified AI tools’ positive roles in project management and governance—through support for (human-led) decision support, transparency, and anticipatory governance—but also revealed tensions around equity, attentional displacement, and the marginalisation of national actors.</jats:p>
publication: The African Journal of Information and Communication (AJIC)

title: Instability absorption by tertiary educators: Technology adoption under conditions of fragility in the Liberian higher education sector
author: Olajide Jolugbo, Agnes Reeves-Taylor
summary: <jats:p>Digital transformation in higher education is frequently framed in terms of access and adoption. Such framings generally failed to consider how digital higher education systems function under conditions of persistent infrastructural instability and constrained institutional capacity. This study examines Liberian educators’ experiences of digital provision under conditions of fragility in the country’s higher education sector. Based on data from interviews and a survey with 22 educators across 11 Liberian tertiary institutions, the research found that continuity is sustained to a great extent not through the provision of technological systems and user acceptance of those systems, but rather through educators’ adaptations to the unstable state of the technological infrastructure. The educators’ responses fall into four main instability absorption categories—responsibility displacement; non-institutional and informal communication infrastructures; communicative labour; and uneven digital labour—and the study proposes the instability absorption model (IAM) to explain how these absorption practices sustain digital education delivery. The model frames technology adoption under conditions of fragility as a process of sustained operationalisation, where systems continue functioning through continuous human absorption of infrastructure disruption.</jats:p>
publication: The African Journal of Information and Communication (AJIC)

title: Bridging global and local influences: Kenya’s emerging approach to AI governance
author: Jeremiah Osida Onunga
summary: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified demand for national AI governance frameworks that balance innovation with ethical, legal, and societal safeguards. Emerging economies such as Kenya face the dual challenge of seeking to foster AI-driven growth while at the same time managing numerous risks. This study explores Kenya’s emerging approach to AI governance, as represented by its Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030 and Artificial Intelligence Bill of 2026. Through policy–legislative content analysis, the study examines the degree to which Kenya’s approach is both transplanting and localising the orientation and provisions of the EU’s influential AI governance instrument, the Artificial Intelligence Act of 2024. The research also applies a contextual-adaptation analysis to examine the extent to which Kenya’s AI governance approach is geared towards its particular national needs.</jats:p>
publication: The African Journal of Information and Communication (AJIC)

title: Negotiating and navigating colourism in Cuba and Ghana: Perspectives represented in the work of Cuban poet Nicolás Guillén and in Ghanaian TikTok and YouTube content
author: Franklina Kabio-Danlebo, Setor Donne Novieto
summary: <jats:p>There is a strong body of literature on colourism—discrimination among people of colour on the basis of darkness or lightness of skin tone—as it has manifested, and continues to manifest, among Black communities in the Americas and Africa. The phenomenon, with its roots in colonialism, is sufficiently powerful to produce a wide range of social, cultural, and economic effects and a wide range of responses, including skin-bleaching practices that can have severe health consequences. This study explores the dynamics of colourism in two national contexts, Cuba and Ghana, which are highly distinct from each other and at the same time both strongly marked by the sociocultural legacies of colonialism, including the phenomenon of colourism. The study examines Cuban colourism as it is explored and combatted in the 1930s poetry of Cuban writer Nicolás Guillén, and Ghanaian colourism as it is both promoted and critiqued in contemporary TikTok and YouTube social-media content.</jats:p>
publication: The African Journal of Information and Communication (AJIC)

title: Digital public infrastructure (DPI) across Africa: A national identity systems perspective
author: Jonathan Klaaren
summary: <jats:p>A rising global politics advocates for national investments in digital public infrastructure (DPI). The national DPI paradigm combines three core elements: digital national identity systems, digital national payment systems, and safe and secure data exchange. This study, grounded in literature on national identity systems and legal identity, assesses digital national identity systems in several African countries. Based on two of the core functions of identity systems (identification, authentication), as well as identity systems’ linkages to national payments systems, the study conceptualises four main types of digital national identity systems present in African countries: identification-led, authentication-led, plural, and payments-led. The study tests the applicability of the typology on a set of 11 African jurisdictions and finds that eight of the jurisdictions fit within the typology: South Africa, Uganda and Zambia (identification-led systems); Ethiopia and Morocco (authentication-led systems); Ghana (plural system); and Kenya and Nigeria (payments-led systems). The study contributes to global DPI debates by emphasising the authentication function in identity systems, by problematising the relationship between national identity systems and payment systems, and by engaging with global DPI indicators.</jats:p>
publication: The African Journal of Information and Communication (AJIC)

title: Retraction: Gopal, A.D. (2025). How web-interface design impacts task performance, cognitive load, and user experience (UX): An exploration with a cohort of South African university students
author: AJIC
summary: <jats:p>This is a retraction of an article that was published in AJIC Issue 36 of 2025.</jats:p>
publication: The African Journal of Information and Communication (AJIC)

title: Is a Bank Account Property Protected by Section 25 of the <i>Constitution</i>? A Constitutional and Doctrinal Analysis
author: Loice Takaedza
summary: In the digital age access to the financial system, gauged primarily by having a bank account, has become fundamental to modern life. The act of opening a bank account establishes a legal relationship between the client and the bank, raising critical questions about the nature and ownership of the account itself. The purpose of this article is to interrogate the legal status of a bank account: What constitutes a bank account and who owns it - the bank or the account holder? The analysis is framed within the context of section 25 of the Constitution, which protects against the arbitrary deprivation and unlawful expropriation of property. The article examines the constitutional meaning of "property" and whether a bank account qualifies for protection under this provision. Central to the inquiry is whether the unilateral closure of a bank account by a bank constitutes an arbitrary deprivation. Notably, the focus is not on the funds credited to the account, which are legally recognised as the property of the bank, but on the bank account itself as a potential property interest. By exploring this area, the article contributes to the broader discourse on financial inclusion, property rights and constitutional protections in a technologically evolving society.

title: Book Review: Patryk I Labuda <i>International Criminal Tribunals and Domestic Accountability: In the Court's Shadow</i> (Oxford University Press 2023) ISBN 978-0-19-886884-2
author: Fungisai Gloria A Gcumeni
summary: In International Criminal Tribunals and Domestic Accountability: In the Court's Shadow, Labuda offers a nuanced analysis of the theoretical concept of complementarity, elucidating its role and significance for domestic accountability in international criminal justice. The book expertly explores International Criminal Tribunals' shadows and how their responses to international crimes are handled at domestic jurisdictions. Empirical case studies concerning Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sierra Leone are investigated in extricating the synergies in the complex interactions of international tribunals and national jurisdictions in addressing international crimes of a serious nature. The relevance of the book is in its evaluation of present attitudes in law and among relevant stakeholders - mainly states and International Criminal Tribunals for robust and effective responses in enforcing international justice.

title: The Legal Duty of Municipalities to Contribute to Estuarine Management in South Africa: The Case of Knysna Local Municipality
author: Viandrie Robertson, Lourens Erasmus
summary: Estuaries are ecological treasures providing a range of environmental and socio-economic benefits to their communities. Yet estuaries are also the most threatened and least protected ecosystems in South Africa. Municipalities are ideally positioned to contribute to estuarine management due to their proximity to their communities and their specific needs; however, the environment, and by implication also estuaries, is a functional competence of national and provincial governments. In addition, local governments themselves are sometimes to blame for the pollution of estuaries within their jurisdictions. The Knysna Estuary is a case in point, where the mismanagement of the local Wastewater Treatment Works by the Knysna Local Municipality is partly to blame for the Estuary's deterioration. The Knysna Estuary is currently under the jurisdiction of the South African National Parks and is the most important estuary in South Africa in terms of conservation. This article examines whether and how municipalities can contribute to estuarine management, with a particular focus on the Knysna Estuary. The authors argue that local government's developmental mandate, coupled with municipalities' obligation to realise the constitutional environmental right, as well as those imposed by the National Environmental Management Act 107 of 1998 and numerous other sector-specific environmental laws, place a duty on municipalities to contribute to estuarine management. They further argue that these laws provide municipalities with the necessary governance tools to perform this function effectively.

title: You Rise and Fall on Your Papers: <i> </i> <i>Plettenberg Bay Ratepayers and Residents Association v Bitou Municipality</i> [2024] ZAWCHC 71
author: Nonhlanhla Ngcobo
summary: The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 (the Constitution), serves as the foundational basis for local government's status, powers and functions, establishing the comprehensive legal framework that governs municiplaities. Section 153 of the Constitution states that a municipality must structure and manage its administration, budgeting and planning processes to give priority to the basic needs of the community. This section is further echoed in the White Paper on Local Government, 1998, which defines a developmental local government as a government that works with local communities to improve their quality of life. In the present case, the applicant (Plettenberg Bay Ratepayers and Residents Association) failed to align their arguments with the legal framework governing local government when challenging the decision of the Municipal Council to purchase luxury vehicles for the use of the executive mayor and their deputy. As a result, the case proved ineffective in addressing the financial behaviour of the Municipal Council and ultimately failed to address the core legal issues. This analysis concludes that the applicant's failure to frame their arguments properly led to two undesired outcomes: an unjust outcome not benefiting the Bitou local community and the opportunity for the court to advance local government scholarship on municipal fiscal powers and their responsibilities.

title: The code of conduct and suspensions and expulsions: BELA Act’s passes and fails
author: Mariëtte Reyneke
summary: The Basic Education Laws Amendment Act (BELA Act) introduced amendments to the South African Schools Act, which came into effect on December 24, 2024. Specifically, sections 8 and 9 of the Schools Act, addressing codes of conduct, disciplinary hearings, suspensions, and expulsions, have faced criticism for insufficient alignment with the constitutional principle of prioritizing the best interests of the child. This article examines the amendments to these sections to assess whether the BELA Act effectively addresses these concerns. The analysis concludes that while the amendments incorporate some judicial precedents and make valuable contributions to the legislation, they fall short of fully promoting the best interests of all learners in school disciplinary processes.

title: Linking Labour Law and Consumer Law in South Africa: The Impact of the “Add Hope Initiative” on KFC Employees and Consumers
author: Mahlatse Innocent Maake-Malatji
summary: This article explores the legal and ethical challenges of corporate-social-responsibility initiatives, focusing on KFC South Africa’s “Add Hope” charity campaign. With South Africa’s ongoing issues of poverty and unemployment, corporate-social-responsibility campaigns, such as soliciting small donations from consumers, can significantly impact employees and consumers alike. The study identifies gaps in South African labour and consumer-protection laws that fail to address fully the pressures placed on employees tasked with soliciting donations and the ethical concerns surrounding consumer coercion. Through doctrinal analysis and case studies, this article examines these issues and calls for a more nuanced legal framework to safeguard both employee welfare and consumer rights. The findings highlight the need for clear legal guidelines regarding corporate-social-responsibility participation and consumer protection from undue influence. This article underscores the importance of establishing a balance between corporate social responsibility and the protection of employee and consumer rights. By revising labour and consumer-protection laws to account for the specific challenges posed by corporate social responsibility, businesses can foster more ethical, transparent and sustainable charitable initiatives. This study contributes to the broader conversation about the intersection of corporate responsibility, labour rights and consumer protection, offering insights that can inform both legal scholarship and policy development.

title: The Delegation of Parliament’s Law-Making Power:  <i>Democratic Alliance v Minister of Co-Operative</i> <i>Governance and Traditional Affairs</i> [2021] ZAGPPHC 168; 2024 (5) SA 463 (SCA)
author: Bradley Slade
summary: Section 27 of the Disaster Management (Act 57 of 2002) (DMA) awards the national executive authority delegated law-making power to effectively manage a disaster, as was the case when the presence of the Coronavirus disease was confirmed in South Africa in March 2020. Although it is accepted that Parliament can delegate law-making power to the national executive authority, the question around the limitations of the power to delegate law-making power was addressed in the High Court and Supreme Court of Appeal decisions in Democratic Alliance v Minister of Co-Operative Governance and Traditional Affairs. The Democratic Alliance attacked the constitutionality of the DMA on the basis that section 27 constitutes and impermissible delegation of law-making power. Furthermore, the Democratic Alliance argued that the DMA is unconstitutional as it does not expressly provide for parliamentary oversight when section 27 is implemented. This case note provides an overview of these decisions and concludes that although it is generally accepted that Parliament can delegate its law-making powers to the executive authority, the extent to which it can do so is strictly considered by the courts. On this basis the courts confirmed the general restrictions that must be in place for the delegation of law-making power to be considered valid. As the DMA contains sufficient safeguards for the exercise of the delegated law-making power, the courts did not find the DMA unconstitutional on this basis. The courts also found that the lack of express provisions in the DMA requiring parliamentary oversight when section 27 is implemented does not render the DMA unconstitutional. However, due to the minority decision in the Supreme Court of Appeal decision, which differed from the majority on this point, Parliament should consider building in express provisions for parliamentary oversight when section 27 is implemented in such a manner that the executive would still be able to deal effectively with a disaster.

title: Fit and Proper: An Analysis of Judicial Precedent
author: Sean Alan Jackson
summary: The legal profession holds a pivotal role in upholding justice, safeguarding public trust, and maintaining the integrity of the judicial system. This stems from the significance of the separation of powers as set out in the Constitution. Central to this mandate is the principle that legal practitioners must meet the “fit and proper” standard outlined in the Legal Practice Act (LPA). This article critically explores various case law highlighting the various professional and ethical obligations of legal practitioners in South Africa. Through an analysis of relevant cases and regulatory frameworks, the article addresses the systemic challenges that undermines these principles and is a reminder that the profession needs more actionable recommendations for reform. The article begins by defining the “fit and proper” that must be maintained throughout a practitioner’s career. Beyond technical expertise, legal practitioners must embody traits such as honesty, diligence, and respect for the rule of law. The failure to uphold these traits can result in disciplinary action, including suspension or being struck off the roll. This standard is essential for preserving the credibility of the legal profession and ensuring public confidence in the administration of justice. One of the key challenges highlighted in the article is the prevalence of ethical lapses within the profession. These lapses are not confined to outright misconduct but often manifest in subtle ways, such as conflicts of interest, poor financial management, and inadequate client communication. Economic pressures, cultural norms, and systemic issues within the profession exacerbate these challenges, creating an environment where ethical compromises may occur. Trust account mismanagement remains a recurring issue as specifically discussed below in the case of the South African Legal Practice Council v Manamela, with some practitioners failing to comply with basic financial regulations. The article emphasizes that such breaches not only harm individual clients but also erode public trust in the profession as a whole. The article also explores the broader implications of ethical behaviour for the legal profession. It argues that ethical breaches have far-reaching consequences, affecting not only individual clients but also the justice system and society at large. For example, cases in this article discuss dishonesty or negligence which can undermine public confidence in the legal system, making it harder for marginalized communities to access justice. Maintaining high ethical standards is not just a professional obligation but a social responsibility, particularly in a country like South Africa, where the legal system plays a crucial role in addressing historical injustices. Addressing systemic challenges, enhancing oversight mechanisms, and emphasizing ethics in education and training are critical for upholding the “fit and proper” standard. By adopting these measures, the profession can safeguard its integrity, protect public trust, and ensure that justice is administered fairly and effectively. Ultimately, the article emphasizes that the sustainability of the legal profession depends on a collective commitment to ethical excellence, making it not only a requirement of the law but also a moral imperative. Comprehensive analysis of case law such as: Heppell v Law Society of the Northern Provinces, General Council of the Bar of South Africa v Jiba and Another, General Council of the Bar of SA v Geach, Legal Practice Council of South Africa v Mamabolo, South African Legal Practice Council v Teffo and numerous important judicial precedent provides valuable insights for practitioners, candidate, and academics, contributing to a deeper understanding of the ethical foundations of the legal profession and their significance in promoting justice. As candidate legal practitioners and legal practitioners navigate their professional responsibilities, it is imperative that they consistent

title: Tolerated, But Never Equal: The Limits Of Recognising Difference
author: Johndré Barnes
summary: The article examines the South African Constitutional Court’s reliance on toleration as a legal mechanism for recognising difference, particularly concerning LGBTQIA+ individuals. While the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, aspires to achieve substantive equality, foster diversity and uphold human dignity, the article argues that the invocation of toleration does not fully realise that vision. Instead, it merely accommodates difference within predefined limits, maintaining entrenched social hierarchies and, in turn, fails to dismantle systemic discrimination. Through an analysis of landmark cases – including National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality v Minister of Justice, National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality v Minister of Home Affairs, and Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie, the article explores how the court frames legal recognition without fully disrupting dominant social norms. It highlights how toleration, while often perceived as a progressive legal mechanism for promoting inclusion and diversity, functions as a conditional and asymmetrical practice in which the dominant group determines the boundaries of what is acceptable. Ultimately, the article critiques the court’s jurisprudence for reinforcing rather than transforming power structures. It argues that toleration results in superficial inclusion – a façade of legal protection that masks deeper structural inequalities. Rather than giving effect to the ideals of the Constitution, toleration operates as a mechanism for regulating full legal and social belonging and limiting true substantive equality.

title: SCA Provides Clarity on the Requirements Needed for the Court to Grant Remedial Action for Oppressive and Unfair Conduct in Terms of Section 163 of the Companies Act 71 of 2008 - Parry v Dunn-Blatch [2024] ZASCA 19
author: Darren Subramanien, Dehal Jivan, Suhail Ebrahim
summary: The “oppression remedy”, while having arguably undergone substantial legislative development over time, has long been a contentious issue for South African courts. The use of this remedy allows shareholders or directors to challenge, and seek relief from, certain acts or omissions they believe are oppressive or unfairly prejudicial, or that unfairly disregard their interests. In Parry v Dunn-Blatch ([2024] ZASCA 19), the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) had to consider whether the act or omission envisaged in section 163(1) of the Companies Act 71 of 2008 (the 2008 Act) had taken place as alleged by the applicant. The decision of the SCA in Parry v Dunn-Blatch (supra) is important as the court provided much-needed clarity as to what will be required by an applicant who wishes to bring a successful application for use of the remedy found in section 163 of the 2008 Act.

title: Competition Law as a Catalyst for Access to Education: A Review of a Drive against Anti-Competitive Practices in the Procurement of School Uniforms by the Competition Commission of South Africa
author: Sandiso Mbulawa
summary: Exclusive agreements and high prices in some markets can harm competition, competitors, and consumers and may also affect the enjoyment of constitutionally protected rights. Some practices impinge on aspects of citizens’ fundamental rights, such as the right of access to education. In response to complaints from parents regarding anti-competitive practices involving schools, suppliers and/or manufacturers, the Competition Commission has undertaken a series of interventions to enhance competition in the procurement of school uniforms and other related materials. The initiative was aimed at promoting and balancing increasing competition in school-uniform procurement and to provide parents with more choices to ensure that they are not compelled to purchase school uniforms exclusively from selected suppliers. The initiative not only achieved market competitiveness, but, to a certain extent, it also secured the constitutional right to access to education. Therefore, the article examines the effectiveness of the Competition Commission’s interventions on the procurement of school uniforms and showcases the role the agency played in promoting access to education.

title: Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 3)
author: Jan-Louis van Tonder
summary: Sections 4(1)(a) and (b) of the Competition Act 89 of 1998 reflect the distinction in competition law between horizontal restrictive practices that may be evaluated either through a “rule of reason” analysis or treated as automatically unlawful under a “per se” approach. Section 4(1)(a) contemplates a “rule of reason” analysis in terms of which the anti-competitive effects of the conduct in issue must be proved and, even if such effects are demonstrated, they are susceptible to justification on technological, efficiency or pro-competitive grounds. By contrast, where the impugned conduct involves any of the restrictive horizontal practices listed in section 4(1)(b), namely, price-fixing, market division or collusive tendering, it is prohibited “per se” in that the anti-competitive effect thereof is presumed and cannot be justified on technological, efficiency or pro-competitive grounds. As is the case with bona fide agreements that are embarked upon by competitors for a legitimate purpose, commercially reasonable ancillary restraints, even when concluded between competitors, ought not to be treated as automatically infringing section 4(1)(b) without further enquiry. For these purposes, the Competition Appeal Court (CAC) in Dawn Consolidated Holdings (Pty) Ltd v Competition Commission (Dawn) has developed a well-refined test to assess whether a restraint of trade within a broader agreement, such as a joint venture, falls within the scope of the prohibitions enacted by section 4(1)(b) of the Competition Act. Part 1 critically reviews the applicable South African framework and principles relevant to characterisation as developed in American Natural Soda Ash Corporation v Competition Commission and Competition Commission v South African Breweries Ltd and assesses the approach to whether conduct is anti-competitive by object or effect under article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (EU). Part 2 builds on Part 1 by reviewing and assessing key facets of characterisation that have further emerged from notable cases such as Aranda Textile Mills (Pty) Ltd v The Competition Commission of South Africa, Tourvest Holdings (Pty) Ltd v Competition Commission, Competition Commission of South Africa v Irwin & Johnson, and Competition Commission v Waco Africa (Pty) Ltd. Part 3 reviews and assesses the approach relevant to characterisation of ancillary restraints of trade as developed by the CAC in Dawn. Pursuant to section 1(3) of the Competition Act, appropriate foreign and international law may be considered when interpreting or applying the Competition Act. This is complementary to section 1(2)(a), which directs that the Competition Act must be interpreted in a manner that is consistent with the Constitution and that gives effect to the purposes set out in section 2. In light hereof, this article also considers the approaches in the United Kingdom, the EU and the United States. (Van Tonder “Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 1)” 2025 46(4) Obiter 872–886; Van Tonder “Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 2)” 2026 47(1) Obiter 1–14)

title: Foreclosure of Primary Home Mortgages in Namibia: Towards Efficient Judicial Oversight
author: PC Nhekairo, NV Asheela-Shikalepo
summary: Mortgage foreclosures represent a significant and contentious issue, particularly when they pertain to individuals’ primary homes. Foreclosure inherently creates a conflict between two opposing interests: the mortgagee’s entitlement to enforce their security and the imperative to alleviate the severe repercussions of displacing the mortgagor and their family, which could lead to homelessness. In Namibia, the relevance of mortgage foreclosure concerning primary homes is exacerbated by a persistent housing crisis; thus, displacing a mortgagor and their family contributes to the alarming statistic that about 25 per cent of the population lacks access to adequate housing. The interplay of interests among the mortgagor, the mortgagee and external entities such as the government necessitates a careful balancing exercise in the enforcement of mortgage foreclosures. The execution of foreclosures on primary homes in Namibia is primarily governed by rule 108 of the High Court Rules, which mandates judicial oversight prior to declaring primary homes specially executable. This article contends that the existing regulatory framework in Namibia does not adequately reconcile the competing interests associated with the foreclosure of primary homes. Based on the results of a comparative analysis, this article ultimately proposes the promulgation of a comprehensive foreclosure regulatory framework.

title: The Constitutional and Legislative Powers of Local Authorities in South Africa: The Applicability of an Ocean Accounts Framework as an Ocean-Governance Instrument
author: Hendrik J Van As
summary:
This research examines the Ocean Accounts Framework (OAF) as an instrument for ocean governance and policy development by South African local authorities. The Constitution imposes sustainable developmental duties on municipalities, requiring them to budget and plan in a way that prioritises basic community needs and promotes social and economic development. With their funding primarily coming from property rates, service surcharges and payments from national government, municipalities are responsible for local economic and infrastructure development, promoting a safe and healthy environment, and service delivery.

Coastal management is the shared responsibility of all three branches of government and frequently overlaps. South Africa adopted the National Development Plan (NDP) to promote economic growth and address the triple challenge of inequality, unemployment and poverty. Operation Phakisa prioritises marine transport, offshore oil and gas, aquaculture and marine protection services. 

This article examines the relationship between the OAF and the legislative and policy instruments that guide coastal and ocean governance in South Africa’s local government sphere. As part of a community of practice (CoP), the research assesses the applicability of the OAF in South Africa and the Western Indian Ocean (WIO), with a focus on the legal context in which the OAF is to be used. It investigates the constitutional and legislative powers and functions of local authorities that are relevant to the blue economy and the extent to which municipalities exercise these powers and functions. It also assesses the OAF’s potential to evaluate food security and sustainability risks for local populations, and whether local authorities can legislate against marine-resource crimes to augment national legislation. Finally, the study argues that using the OAF to measure ocean value for municipal development could boost funding and help local authorities meet the requirements set by the Constitution, the NDP and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Local authorities should realise the importance of the ocean and its living resources and use a credible valuation tool to exercise their legislative powers.

title: Unconstitutional Transitions or Constitutions without Constitutionalism in Africa? A Review of Cameroon and Gabon Experiences
author: Elisabeth Achancho Etagha
summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>African constitutional practice continues to grapple with challenges of political instability and contested legitimacy. This article critically examines the tension between unconstitutional transitions and constitutions without constitutionalism in Africa, with a particular focus on the experiences of Cameroon and Gabon. It explores how formal constitutional frameworks, while outwardly adhering to legal norms, have been systematically manipulated to entrench authoritarian rule and undermine democratic legitimacy. Drawing on constitutional texts, legal reforms, and political events from both countries, the article distinguishes between de facto unconstitutional changes of government and de jure constitutional orders that nonetheless contravene fundamental democratic principles. The analysis employs a comparative constitutional methodology, supplemented by political theory and historical context, to evaluate the extent to which constitutions in these cases serve as instruments of democratic governance or authoritarian consolidation. The research reveals that in both cases, constitutional frameworks have been strategically modified to legitimise authoritarian rule, blurring the line between legality and illegitimacy. It calls for a reconceptualisation of constitutional practice in Africa, one that moves beyond formal legality toward substantive democratic norms rooted in accountability, participation, and human rights.</jats:p>

title: The House of Representatives of Zanzibar’s Encroachment on Union Constitutional Legislative Powers in Tanzania
author: Ryoba Marwa
summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This Article examines the constitutional legal framework governing the division of legislative powers between the Union Parliament and the House of Representatives of Zanzibar within the United Republic of Tanzania. The United Republic of Tanzania operates under a unique constitutional arrangement that combines elements of both federalism and unitary governance. The study employed doctrinal analysis to examine how the House of Representatives of Zanzibar has encroached upon the Union Parliament’s legislative powers, thereby contravening the supremacy of the Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania. This study revealed that the House of Representatives of Zanzibar has consistently exceeded its legislative powers, despite constitutional limits, by passing laws on ports, maritime exclusive economic zones, and petroleum resources, all of which are classified as Union Matters. This creates legal uncertainty, administrative duplication, enforcement fragmentation and jeopardises the integrity of the Union. The study concludes that these legislative intrusions contravene the principle of constitutional supremacy and recommends constitutional reform to strengthen safeguards against jurisdictional overlap and to align enacted laws with the Union’s constitutional supremacy.</jats:p>

title: <i>The Routledge Handbook of Cultural Legal Studies</i>
author: Isolde de Villiers

title: <i>The Literary Exception and the Rule of Law</i>: a conversation on liberal democracy, populism, interpretation, law and poetry
author: Johan van der Walt, Karin van Marle, Wessel le Roux
summary: Johan van der Walt discusses key themes from his most recent book The Literary Exception and the Rule of Law Oxfordshire Routledge (2023) with Karin van Marle and Wessel le Roux. Van der Walt calls for a genre of law and literature scholarship that does not seek to soften or erase the differences between law and literature, as is typical in most law-as-literature scholarship, but that seeks to highlight the tensions between law and literature (represented by the avant garde poetry of Paul Celan and Paul Valéry). Van der Walt argues that the same event can give rise to a legal and a poetic response. Liberal society exists in the space that is opened up by these opposing trajectories. Liberal law must respect the non-poetic nature of its regulatory function and resist attempts, especially among nationalists and populists, to cure the existential inadequacy of law.
